[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Feature Scaling and Normalization in Machine Learning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Feature scaling is a crucial preprocessing step in machine learning that standardizes the range of independent variables or features of data. Since data collected from various sources often comes in different scales and units, scaling ensures that all features contribute equally to the model's performance."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Why is Feature Scaling Necessary?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Many machine learning algorithms, such as Gradient Descent-based algorithms (Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Neural Networks) and distance-based algorithms (K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machines, K-Means Clustering), are sensitive to the magnitude of features."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Gradient Descent: Unscaled features result in elongated cost function contours, making gradient descent oscillate and converge much slower."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Distance Metrics: Algorithms like KNN compute Euclidean distances. A feature with a larger numerical range will dominate the distance calculation over features with smaller ranges."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Common Techniques for Feature Scaling"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"There are two primary techniques used for feature scaling: Normalization (Min-Max Scaling) and Standardization (Z-score Normalization)."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Normalization (Min-Max Scaling)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Normalization rescales the features to a fixed range, usually between 0 and 1. This is particularly useful when the data does not follow a Gaussian distribution and the minimum and maximum boundaries are known."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"X_scaled = (X - X_min) / (X_max - X_min)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Standardization (Z-score Normalization)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Standardization centers the features around zero with a standard deviation of one. It transforms the data to have a mean (mu) of 0 and a standard deviation (sigma) of 1. This method is less affected by outliers compared to Min-Max scaling."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"X_scaled = (X - mean(X)) / std(X)"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Python Implementation using Scikit-Learn"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following Python code demonstrates how to apply Min-Max Scaling and Standardization using the scikit-learn library."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler

# Sample data: [Age, Income]
data = np.array([[25, 50000], [32, 75000], [47, 120000], [51, 140000]])

# Apply Min-Max Scaling
min_max_scaler = MinMaxScaler()
data_normalized = min_max_scaler.fit_transform(data)
print("Normalized Data (0 to 1):")
print(data_normalized)

# Apply Standardization
standard_scaler = StandardScaler()
data_standardized = standard_scaler.fit_transform(data)
print("\nStandardized Data (Mean=0, Std=1):")
print(data_standardized)"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Feature Scaling"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always fit the scaler ONLY on the training data to prevent data leakage from the test set."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Transform both the training set and the validation/test sets using the parameters computed from the training set."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Tree-based models (Decision Trees, Random Forests, XGBoost) do not require feature scaling because they split nodes based on feature values rather than distances or gradients."}]
